It may be triggered by a new information request from users, an environmental change such as a reduced budget, a periodic review, or respondent feedback. Action plans from evaluations of previous iterations of the production cycle (including from respondent feedback) or from other programmes might provide an input to this sub-process. It also includes consideration of practice amongst other (national and international) statistical organisations producing similar data and the methods used by those organisations.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process includes the initial investigation and identification of what statistics are needed and what is needed of the statistics. In the modern process, AI and automated tools are used to continuously scan for new information requests from users, detect relevant environmental changes, and aggregate respondent feedback and evaluation action plans. These technologies also benchmark needs by automatically referencing practices among other (national and international) statistical organizations. Automation supports the collation, analysis, and structuring of these triggers for new or changed statistics, while staff focus their expertise on interpreting context, confirming significance, and ensuring response to complex or emergent requirements.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Junior Evaluation Officer' is implicated because they are responsible for 'conducting literature and data research, identifying, gathering, analyzing and synthesizing quantitative and qualitative data' and 'provides input on the interpretation of data to support findings and conclusions.' With automated identification, their role transitions to expert oversight of AI-processed needs data, contextual interpretation, and strategic confirmation.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Consult and confirm needs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process focuses on consulting with the internal and external stakeholders and confirming in detail the needs for the statistics. A good understanding of user needs is required so that the statistical organisation knows not only what it is expected to deliver, but also when, how, and perhaps most importantly, why. For the second and subsequent iterations of this sub-process, the main focus will be on determining whether previously identified needs have changed. This detailed understanding of user needs is the critical part of this sub-process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process focuses on consulting with internal and external stakeholders and confirming in detail the needs for the statistics. Automated and AI-supported systems are now used to organize and analyze input from stakeholders, including feedback, evolving requirements, and historical engagement. These tools facilitate discovery of patterns and highlight changes in user needs over time. Statistical staff engage directly where nuanced negotiation, detailed interpretation, or complex prioritization is required, ensuring that automated summaries and analytics are supplemented by expert, context-aware judgment. This detailed understanding of user needs and the efficient, technology-enabled consultation process are both critical to this sub-process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Junior Evaluation Officer,' who 'participates in the conduct of interviews, and focus groups, applying analytical tools,' and 'provides support in the assessment of current and future requirements for data,' is heavily implicated. Their skills in direct consultation now focus on high-value interpretation of stakeholder input and guiding strategic negotiation—overseeing, validating, and finalizing outputs from automated synthesis.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Establish output objectives
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process identifies the statistical output objectives that are required to meet the user needs confirmed in sub-process 1.2 (Consult and confirm needs). It includes agreeing the suitability of the proposed outputs and their quality measures with users. Legal or normative frameworks (e.g. relating to confidentiality, methodologies), and available resources are important to consider when establishing output objectives.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process identifies the statistical output objectives that are required to meet the user needs confirmed in sub-process 1.2 (Consult and confirm needs). AI and automated tools aggregate and analyze confirmed user requirements, historical deliverables, legal/normative frameworks, and available resource constraints to generate draft output objectives and candidate quality measures. Staff provide oversight by aligning these drafts with strategic intent, adjudicating complex trade-offs, and ensuring compliance with legal and methodological expectations. This shift supports more efficient, responsive, and high-quality output objective-setting by leveraging technology for foundational work and human expertise for final judgment and alignment.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Junior Evaluation Officer' 'participates... to evaluate... performance' and 'provides input on the interpretation of data to support findings and conclusions,' making them responsible for reviewing and confirming automated draft objectives, assessing quality, and contextualizing outputs.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Prepare and submit business case
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase, in the form of a business case to get approval to implement the new or modified statistical business process. Such a business case would need to conform to the requirements of the approval body, but would typically include elements such as: A description of the “As-Is” business process (if it already exists), with information on how the current statistics are produced, highlighting any inefficiencies and issues to be addressed; The proposed “To-Be” solution, detailing how the statistical business process will be developed to produce the new or revised statistics; An assessment of costs and benefits against objectives and any external constraints. The business case describes options and makes recommendations. It may include the benefits, costs, deliverables, time frame, budget, required technical and human resources, risk assessment and impact on stakeholders for each option. After the business case is prepared, it is submitted for approval to move to the next phase of the business process. At this sub-process, a “go”/“no go” decision is made. Typically, the business case is reviewed and formally approved or disapproved by the appropriate sponsors and governance committees.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase in the form of a business case to get approval to implement a new or modified statistical business process. In the contemporary process, automated and AI-driven systems are used to collate, analyze, and generate initial drafts for all key business case sections—including the description of the 'As-Is' process, the proposed 'To-Be' solution, and the relevant assessments of cost, benefit, risks, deliverables, and impact. Staff and sponsors then review, contextualize, and refine these drafts, ensuring proper alignment with strategic objectives and organizational needs before final submission. The business case is reviewed and approved by the relevant body, with human expertise providing the final evaluation and decision. By leveraging automation, the preparation of business cases gains efficiency and speed, allowing human effort to be concentrated on strategic oversight and quality assurance.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Junior Evaluation Officer,' whose work-description specifies 'provides the Evaluation Manager with supporting data for sections of reports, presentations, briefing notes and memoranda for senior management on elements of program evaluations of various programs,' and 'conducts analyses and interpretation of data collected during evaluation studies under the supervision of the Evaluation Manager,' is now focused on critically reviewing, supplementing, and validating drafted business case materials produced by automation, ensuring they are strategically sound for decision making.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Evaluate
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This phase manages the evaluation of a specific instance of a statistical business process, as opposed to the more general overarching activity of Quality Management described in Section V (Descriptions of overarching activities). It can take place at the end of the instance of the process, but can also be done on an ongoing basis during the statistical production process. It relies on inputs gathered throughout the different phases. It includes evaluating the success of a specific instance of the statistical business process, drawing on a range of quantitative and qualitative inputs, and identifying and prioritising potential improvements. For statistical outputs produced regularly, evaluation should, at least in theory, occur for each iteration, determining whether future iterations should take place, and if so, whether any improvements should be implemented. However, in some cases, particularly for regular and wellestablished statistical business processes, evaluation might not be formally carried out for each iteration. In such cases, this phase can be seen as providing the decision as to whether the next iteration should start from the Specify Needs phase, or from some later phase (often the Collect phase). The Evaluate phase is broken down into three sub-processes (Figure 14), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This phase manages evaluation for each statistical business process instance using automation and AI/LLM-powered pipelines for gathering, synthesizing, and analyzing all feedback and performance metrics. Iterative, digital-first workflows continuously update and surface actionable insights, with automated reports and dashboards flagging opportunities for adjustment, learning, and quality enhancement. Human analysts focus on contextual review, recommendation adjudication, and final sign-off of improvement plans for future iterations. Evaluation may occur at the end or during any process cycle, and is broken into three sub-processes (Figure 14) which may run simultaneously or be repeated until required standards are met.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The updated GSBPM requires that 'evaluation is a digital, AI-driven, and iterative process that continuously aggregates feedback, quality metrics, and performance data from all stages.' The 'Junior Evaluation Officer', whose duties include 'participates as a member of project teams in the conduct of evaluation studies,' 'undertakes assigned tasks related to specific elements of evaluation projects such as, conducting literature and data research, identifying, gathering, analyzing and synthesizing quantitative and qualitative data,' and 'provides input on the interpretation of data to support findings and conclusions,' will be increasingly responsible for reviewing, interpreting, and contextualizing results generated by AI/LLM-driven evaluation pipelines. Rather than manually aggregating and reviewing feedback, they will focus on deeper interpretation, prioritization of actionable recommendations, and providing final input or oversight in the evaluation cycle.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Gather evaluation inputs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: Evaluation material can be produced in any other phase or sub-process. It may take many forms, including feedback from users, process metadata (paradata), system metrics, and staff suggestions. Reports of progress against an action plan agreed during a previous iteration may also form an input to evaluations of subsequent iterations. This sub-process gathers all of these inputs, compiles quality indicators and makes them available for the person or team producing the evaluation. The collection of some of these evaluation materials can be automated and take place in a continuous way throughout the whole process, as defined by the quality framework (see Quality Management in Section V). On the other hand, for the evaluation of certain processes it can be necessary to perform specific activities such as small surveys, (e.g. post-enumeration surveys, re-interview studies, survey on effectiveness of dissemination).
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: Evaluation input gathering is orchestrated via automated, AI/LLM-powered systems that harvest, aggregate, and cluster all feedback, process-metadata, quality metrics, and staff input in real time. Inputs are continuously updated and synthesized for use in ongoing and cyclical evaluation phases, easing the workload on evaluators and ensuring the highest possible input quality and completeness for downstream analysis and decision-making.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: GSBPM specifies that all feedback, suggestions, and metrics are now 'automatically collected and synthesized by LLMs and digital/AI platforms.' The 'Junior Evaluation Officer,' who must 'collect diverse data and information from a variety of sources,' 'undertake literature and data research in support of evaluation studies,' and 'analyze and interpret data collected during evaluation studies,' is now focused on interpreting aggregated and synthesized AI-generated inputs and ensuring that input quality and relevance are maintained for rapidly-iterative evaluation cycles.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Conduct evaluation
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process analyses the evaluation inputs, compares them to the expected/target benchmarking results (when available), and synthesises them into an evaluation report or control dashboard. The evaluation can take place at the end of the whole process (ex-post evaluation), for selected activities, during its execution in a continuous way, or throughout the process, thus allowing for quick fixes or continuous improvement. The resulting report should note any quality issues specific to this iteration of the statistical business process as well as highlighting any deviation of performance metrics from expected values, and should make recommendations for changes if appropriate. These recommendations can cover changes to any phase or sub-process for future iterations of the process, or can suggest that the process is not repeated.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process analyzes evaluation inputs using LLM/AI-powered digital evaluation algorithms. Automated benchmarking, synthesis, and reporting produce dashboards, quality issues lists, and draft improvement recommendations for each statistical production iteration. Human experts review AI-generated outputs, contextualize findings, and finalize the recommendations and improvement plans to be carried out in current or future cycles.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: GSBPM requires that evaluation is 'undertaken by LLM/AI-driven processes, which analyze synthesized feedback, benchmark outcomes, and draft improvement recommendations.' The 'Junior Evaluation Officer', who had previously manually analyzed evaluation data, now oversees the interpretation, refinement, and contextualization of AI-produced evaluation reports, identifies high-impact issues or improvement opportunities, and provides senior-level recommendations based on AI findings.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Agree an action plan
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process brings together the necessary decision-making power to form and agree an action plan based on the evaluation report. It should also include consideration of a mechanism for monitoring the impact of those actions, which may, in turn, provide an input to evaluations of future iterations of the process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process brings together digital and AI-supported platforms for drafting, recommending, and monitoring action plans based on the synthesized evaluation. Automated dashboards and traceable tracking systems surface plan effectiveness and support human decision-makers in approving, customizing, and finalizing future improvement actions. Ongoing digital monitoring ensures that the impacts of each action feed directly into subsequent evaluation cycles, creating a robust loop of continuous improvement.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: GSBPM: 'Action planning is digital and AI-driven, with action proposals, tracking, and follow-through reporting all handled by automated solutions.' The 'Junior Evaluation Officer', who 'provides input on the interpretation of data to support findings and conclusions' and 'recommends enhancements to methods,' is now focused on reviewing, contextualizing, and finalizing AI-generated action plans, suggesting adjustment for context, and validating that monitoring mechanisms are effectively built in for future cycles.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments and operational processes, with due regard to other requirements such as security. It includes all the design elements needed to define or refine the statistical products or services identified in the business case. This phase specifies all relevant metadata, in accordance with the standards and corporate policies, ready for use later in the business process, as well as quality assurance procedures. For statistical outputs produced on a regular basis, this phase usually occurs for the first iteration and whenever improvement actions are identified in the Evaluate phase of a previous iteration. Design activities make substantial use of international and national standards in order to reduce the length and cost of the design process, and enhance interoperability, comparability, etc. Organisations may reuse or adapt design elements from existing processes and consider geospatial aspects of data in the design to enhance the usability and value of the statistical information. Additionally, outputs of design processes may form the basis for future standards at the organisational, national or international levels. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 8), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative. Some approaches used to develop tools and systems involve iteration between sub-processes in the Design and Build phases.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments, and operational processes—with a strong emphasis on automation, AI-powered tools, and digital interoperability. Automated and AI-driven processes play a central role in drafting specifications, aligning with corporate and international standards, generating and enriching metadata, simulating system interactions, and iterating design improvements. All statistical products and their supporting metadata are produced in standardized, richly described, and machine-actionable forms, ensuring they are interoperable and reusable across downstream tools, APIs, and organizational systems. Staff are freed from repetitive and routine design work and instead focus on innovation, calibration, and optimizing for evolving user and stakeholder requirements. Design activities thus promote efficiency, quality, and discoverability, embedding best practices for automation, standardization, and open data access. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 8), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, can occur in parallel, and may be iterative. Iteration between Design and Build phases is supported through automated versioning and process enhancements.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The phase now requires 'automation and AI' for drafting, standards synthesis, metadata creation, and versioning; all outputs must be 'richly described, and machine-actionable,' and staff must be adept at reviewing and contextualizing automated design outputs. The 'Metadata Production and Dissemination Officer' is core to this, as their work includes 'preparing, editing, validating and disseminating statistical metadata,' and 'provides input to documentation, procedures manuals and training manuals related to the production and dissemination of statistical metadata.' Their work will now focus less on manual documentation/metadata production and more on reviewing, adapting, and improving AI/automation-generated metadata and outputs, driving digital transformation and interoperability.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design outputs and dissemination
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process contains the detailed design of the statistical outputs, products and services to be produced, including the related systems, tools and procedures used in the Disseminate phase. Processes governing access to any confidential outputs are also designed here. Outputs should be designed to follow existing standards wherever possible, so inputs to this process may include metadata from similar or previous collections (including extractions from statistical, administrative, geospatial and other non-statistical registers and databases), international standards, and information about practices in other statistical organisations from sub-process 1.1 (Identify needs). Outputs may also be designed in partnership with other interested bodies, particularly if they are considered to be joint outputs, or they will be disseminated by another organisation.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process contains the detailed design of the statistical outputs, products, and services to be produced, including all systems, tools, and procedures to be used in dissemination. Automated and AI-supported solutions are used wherever possible to produce initial output templates, align with existing standards, generate metadata, and configure dissemination tools, allowing staff to focus on innovative features and context-specific requirements, including confidentiality. All outputs and dissemination artifacts must be standardized, richly described, and machine-actionable, with support for APIs, comprehensive metadata tagging, and open formats to maximize interoperability, discoverability, and reusability by human and machine clients. The process includes an explicit, early review of the type and necessity of products, especially visualizations, with the expectation that only those genuinely required for user value or compliance are designed—allowing exclusion where end-users can self-serve or alternatives suffice. Outputs may also be designed in partnership with external organizations, ensuring full alignment with digital-to-digital workflows and standards.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: Digital automation, standards, and metadata-rich, machine-actionable products are now required. The 'Metadata Production and Dissemination Officer''s focus on 'preparing, editing, validating and disseminating statistical metadata,' as well as contributing to 'documentation, procedures manuals and training manuals,' is reoriented toward the oversight of automation-driven, standards-based design outputs, ensuring discoverability, API compatibility, and proper metadata linkage in digital dissemination environments.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design variables
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process defines the variables to be collected via the collection instrument, as well as any other variables that will be derived from them in sub-process 5.5 (Derive new variables and units), and any statistical or geospatial classifications that will be used. This is also where unit types (including observation units and statistical units) can be designed. It is expected that existing national and international standards will be followed wherever possible. This sub-process may need to run in parallel with sub-process 2.3 (Design collection), as the definition of the variables to be collected and the choice of collection instruments may be inter-dependent to some degree. Preparation of metadata for collected and derived variables, statistical and geospatial classification is a necessary precondition for subsequent phases.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process defines the variables to be collected via the collection instrument and any that will be derived for analysis or dissemination, with a strong emphasis on standards compliance, automation, and machine-actionability. All variable definitions and supporting metadata must comply with national and international standards (e.g., SDMX), structured in machine-actionable formats and managed through prescribed data management tools (such as Aria or Colectica) to ensure robust lifecycle control and digital traceability. AI/LLM-enabled tools are used to generate, refine, and validate variable names, descriptions, and attributes, maximizing clarity, standardization, and discoverability. Staff involved in this sub-process are proficient in digital metadata standards and tooling, ensuring all variable-related products are interoperable, automation-ready, and reusable by both human and machine users. This ensures that the resulting statistical outputs are consistently described, easily found, and seamlessly integrated across digital platforms and systems.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The need for 'full standards compliance (SDMX and prescribed tools),' 'AI/LLM-enabled tooling for the automated generation, refinement, and validation of variable descriptions and attributes,' and staff 'proficiency in digital metadata standards and tooling' puts the 'Metadata Production and Dissemination Officer' in a central position: 'prepares, edits, validates and disseminates statistical metadata,' and 'assists with statistical metadata quality evaluations.' The officer's expertise is now directed at supervising AI generation of variable descriptions and ensuring standards and metadata completeness in digital repositories, and documenting/validating digital variable management.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Finalise collection
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process includes loading the collected data and metadata into a suitable electronic environment for further processing. It may include manual or automatic data capture, for example, using clerical staff or optical character recognition tools to extract information from paper questionnaires, or converting the formats of files or encoding the variables received from other organisations. It may also include analysis of the metadata and paradata associated with collection to ensure the collection activities have met requirements. In cases where there is a physical collection instrument, such as a paper questionnaire, which is not needed for further processing, this sub-process manages the archiving of that material. When the collection instrument uses software such as an API or an app, this sub-process also includes the versioning and archiving of these. The data could be pseudonymised at this stage before further processing.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process includes loading the collected data and metadata into a suitable electronic environment for further processing, powered by AI/ML-driven validation and enrichment routines to ensure all metadata repositories and IM tagging are complete, current, and machine-actionable. Routine automatic checks identify and close metadata gaps, verify data structure and governance needs, and prepare files for downstream processing. Finalization is continuously informed by internal and external research, pilot experiments, innovation forums, and evidence-based best practices—enabling iterative improvement and world-leading quality assurance. The subject matter sponsor holds sole responsibility for certifying and accepting the finalized collection data, while operational staff focus on automation, routine execution, and surfacing improvement ideas and lessons learned. Archiving, versioning, and legal compliance handling are embedded as standard, digital-first procedures, ensuring data and metadata are always audit- and analysis-ready.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: Collection finalization must now feature 'automated and AI/ML routines for validating and enriching metadata,' operate as an 'iterative, innovation-driven step,' and assign the subject matter sponsor as responsible for certification/acceptance. The 'Metadata Production and Dissemination Officer'—who is responsible for 'preparing, editing, validating and disseminating statistical metadata,' 'providing input to reports for clients and management,' and 'compiling information from diverse sources in order to prepare, edit, validate and evaluate statistical metadata'—will now handle/validate automated QA and AI-enriched metadata at finalization, advise on iterative improvements, and oversee digital processes for collection certification. Their domain expertise now shifts even more toward review, innovation recommendations, and improving automated QA effectiveness.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Finalise data files
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process brings together the results of the other sub-processes in this phase in a data set (either micro- or macro-data), which is used as the input to the Analyse phase. Sometimes, this may be an intermediate rather than a final data set, particularly for business processes where there are strong time pressures, and a requirement to produce both preliminary and final estimates.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process brings together and finalizes the results of all previous sub-processes in the phase, producing data files (micro- or macro-level) in fully standardized, open, and machine-actionable formats by default. All datasets and supporting documentation are versioned, digitally logged, and immediately available for reproducible handoff to subsequent analysis or dissemination phases. Technical staff ensure compliance with standards and continuous skills development, and all processes are supported by automated documentation and audit trails, supporting immediate traceability, interoperability, and readiness for deployment across business domains.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: All finalized datasets must be 'fully standardized, open, machine-actionable,' with 'automated logs and audit trails, and outputs compatible with human and machine consumers.' The 'Metadata Production and Dissemination Officer'—who 'prepares, edits, validates and disseminates statistical metadata,' and 'analyzes changes in methods, procedures and systems... to determine where updates are required...'—is critically involved to ensure metadata compliance, documentation, and integrity of all final datasets, and to facilitate automated transfer to next processes.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Update output systems
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process manages the update of systems (e.g. databases) where data and metadata are stored ready for dissemination purposes, including: Formatting data and metadata ready to be put into output systems; Loading data and metadata into output systems; Ensuring data are linked to the relevant metadata. Formatting, loading and linking of metadata should preferably mostly take place in earlier phases, but this sub-process includes a final check that all of the necessary metadata are in place ready for dissemination.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process manages the update of output systems and databases for dissemination using automated, real-time loading of data and enriched metadata. Machine-actionable formatting, digital linkage, and metadata validation are built-in, ensuring that all disseminated products are AI- and API-consumable, searchable, and enriched with discoverability standards. Final checks for completeness and metadata enrichment are automatic, and all outputs are designed for seamless use by both human and digital consumers.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Metadata Production and Dissemination Officer' ('prepares, edits, validates and disseminates statistical metadata, ensuring that it is correctly loaded to the corporate metadata repository.') will take primary responsibility for metadata completeness, tag consistency, and API-readiness at the point of output system update.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design collection
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process prepares a collection strategy for the data, and determines the most appropriate collection instruments and methods, which may depend on the type of data collection, the collection unit type (enterprise, person, or other) and the available sources of data. The actual activities in this sub-process will vary according to the type of collection instrument required, which can include computer assisted interviewing, paper questionnaires, administrative registers, automated and semi-automated data transfer methods (such as using APIs, machine-to-machine integrations and various types of file transfers), web-scraping technologies as well as technology for geospatial data. The collection may employ a multi-mode method which requires additional considerations such as design of sequencing or different instruments for different modes. Direct or indirect use of administrative data may be introduced in the data collection mode for either controlling survey data or assisting it when capturing survey information. In the case of survey (or census) data, this collection strategy includes the design of the collection instruments, questions and response templates (in conjunction with the variables and statistical classifications designed in sub-process 2.2 (Design variables)). It is important to understand respondents and incorporate the user perspectives in the design of data collection. This sub-process may include design of fieldwork operations, and respondent engagement, in the case of survey data collection. It also includes the confirmation of existing agreements or creation of new agreements. This sub-process is enabled by tools such as question libraries (to facilitate the reuse of questions and related attributes), questionnaire tools (to enable the quick and easy compilation of questions into formats suitable for cognitive testing) and agreement templates (to help standardise terms and conditions). This sub-process also includes the design of respondent management systems that are specific to this business process. Where statistical organisations do not collect data directly (i.e. a third party controls the collection and processing of the data), this sub-process may include the design of mechanisms to monitor the data and the metadata to assess impacts of any change made by the third party.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process prepares a collection strategy for the data and determines the most appropriate collection instruments and methods, with a strategic emphasis on automation, AI/ML, and passive acquisition. Where possible, the design must prioritize passive, administrative, and already-available sources of data; surveys or direct solicitation are employed only when all other avenues are exhausted or cannot provide suitable data. All aspects of collection design—including the configuration of instruments, sequencing, respondent communications, and integration agreements—should embed automation, machine-to-machine interfaces, digital event/trigger-based collection, and minimal manual intervention. Where a survey instrument is essential, automated and AI-driven methods must be used for design, rendering, and fielding, ensuring quick turnaround, reduced burden, and full standards compliance. The sub-process also entails the necessary design of respondent management, monitoring, and adaptive feedback loops to maximize efficiency and data quality, while reserving human staff for exception handling and final validation.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: Now that collection design must 'prioritize passive, administrative, and already-available sources of data,' and automate 'design, rendering, and fielding' using AI where surveys are required, the 'Operations Officer' is critical: 'Participates in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of manual and automated operations for the collection, coding and processing of data,' 'evaluates collection and coding methods, procedures and results and recommends alternatives.' Their work will change as routine strategy and operational design become increasingly automated. The officer is more focused on ensuring collection design incorporates these new priorities for automation, digital integration (APIs, passive sources), and compliance with passive-first policies.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design frame and sample
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process applies especially to processes which involve data collection based on sampling, such as through statistical surveys, but it may also apply to other types of data collection such as census or register-based (e.g., filtering of registers based on the target population). It identifies and specifies the population of interest, defines a sampling frame (and, where necessary, the register from which it is derived), and determines the most appropriate sampling criteria and methodology (which could include complete enumeration). Common sources for a sampling frame are administrative and statistical registers, censuses and information from other sample surveys. It may refer to geospatial data and classifications. This sub-process describes how these sources can be combined if needed. Analysis of whether the frame covers the target population should be performed. Spatial analysis techniques can be used to ensure the spatial distribution of the units is appropriate. A sampling plan should be made. The actual sample is created in sub-process 4.1 (Create frame and select sample), using the methodology specified in this sub-process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process, which applies to all statistical processes involving sampling, is built around digital automation, flexibility, and data quality by design. Whenever frames or registers from administrative, alternative, or partner-held sources are used, partners are expected and supported to apply AI-driven data cleaning and quality control processes prior to data ingestion by Statistics Canada—improving coverage, comparability, and downstream analytic value. The specification of the population of interest, development of the sampling frame, and establishment of sampling criteria and methodology are designed for full integration with end-to-end digital pipelines, supporting automated and seamless flow between pre-collection and post-collection business processes, drastically reducing manual involvement and risk of programmatic 'patches.' Sampling designs must explicitly allow for a range of dynamic and flexible options (including person-based and adaptive sampling), with supporting digital tools enabling real-time optimization informed by diverse data realities and program goals. This ensures the most efficient, quality-driven, and responsive sampling methodologies possible.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Operations Officer' 'participates in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of manual and automated operations'; the knowledge areas cited include the 'concepts, methods and techniques used in the management and control of statistical collection, coding and processing activities.' As sampling designs must now support 'dynamic and flexible options (including person-based),' and as pipeline integration is prioritized, their practical, systems-based knowledge and focus on operational feasibility and integration is increasingly central.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design production systems and workflows
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process determines the workflow from data collection to dissemination, taking an overview of all the processes required within the whole production process and ensuring that they fit together efficiently with no gaps or redundancies. Various systems and databases may be needed throughout the process. The GSBPM can be used to design a statistical organisation’s business architecture layer when a statistical organisation has an existing enterprise architecture in place. The design might be adjusted to fit the organisation. A general principle is to reuse processes and technology across many statistical business processes, so existing production solutions (e.g. services, systems and databases) should be examined first, to determine whether they are fit for purpose for this specific production process, then, if any gaps are identified, new solutions can be designed. This sub-process also considers how staff will interact with systems and who will be responsible for what and when.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process determines the workflow from data collection to dissemination, ensuring all production processes are seamlessly integrated, modular, and event-driven, with automation and AI/ML supporting orchestration, monitoring, and transitions. Workflows are designed to minimize manual intervention and maximize real-time coordination, leveraging digital platforms and automation for every routine or standardized task. The emphasis is on building touchless, continuous data pipelines that allow for automated validation, routing, escalation, and exception reporting. Existing automated solutions and system components are reused wherever possible; if new components are needed, they are built automation- and integration-ready from inception. Staff responsibilities focus on system oversight, addressing exceptions and inefficiencies, and iteratively improving and upgrading automated workflows for future resilience and scalability.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: With 'modular, event-driven, and AI-enabled workflows for the entirety of the statistical production process' now a requirement, the 'Operations Officer'—responsible for 'participating in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of manual and automated operations for the collection, coding and processing of data,' and for 'analyzing and preparing reports for program managers... problems encountered in implementing concepts, definitions, classifications and other instructions, and recommending alternatives'—must now prioritize automation, modularity, and reusability in designing systems and workflows, as well as ongoing operational quality assurance under highly automated, digitally orchestrated settings.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Build
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This phase builds and tests the production solution to the point where it is ready for use in the 'live' environment. The outputs of the Design phase are assembled and configured in this phase to create the complete operational environment to run the process. New services are built by exception, created in response to gaps in the existing catalogue of services sourced from within the organisation and externally. These new services are constructed to be broadly reusable in alignment with the business architecture of the organisation where possible, and compliant with security requirements. For statistical outputs produced on a regular basis, this phase usually occurs for the first iteration, following a review or a change in methodology or technology, rather than for every iteration. The Build phase is broken down into seven sub-processes (Figure 9), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative. Some approaches used to develop tools and systems involve iteration between sub-processes in the Design and Build phases. The first three sub-processes are concerned with the development and improvement of systems used in collection, processing, analysis and dissemination of data. The last four subprocesses focus on the end-to-end process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This phase builds and tests the production solution to the point where it is ready for use in the 'live' environment, leveraging modular automation and AI-driven assembly at every step. The outputs of the Design phase are assembled and configured using digital orchestration pipelines that prioritize reusability, traceability, and compliance with business architecture and security requirements. Automated configuration, integration, and self-testing are employed wherever possible, enabling rapid, reliable, and consistent system deployment. Human expertise is reserved for overseeing automated processes, handling exceptions that cannot be resolved by automation, and driving continuous improvement in modular service creation. New services are developed only to fill gaps, and are built from inception for automation compatibility, modularity, and compliance. The Build phase is structured into seven sub-processes (Figure 9), supporting iteration and parallelization, and is tightly integrated with Design to ensure seamless translation of specifications into robust operational environments.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The GSBPM update for the Build phase emphasizes 'modular automation and AI-driven assembly at every step,' with automated configuration, integration, and self-testing prioritized. The 'Operations Officer' plays a central role, as their responsibilities include 'participates in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of manual and automated operations for the collection, coding and processing of data' and 'provides assistance and advice to users on methods and practices of collection and coding.' Now, the officer's focus will be on validating, supervising, and adapting increasingly automated, digital system assemblies and integrations, ensuring proper configuration and compliance with automation-first practices.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Reuse or build collection instruments
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process describes the activities to build and reuse the collection instruments needed during the Collect phase. The collection instruments are built based on the design specifications created during the Design phase. A collection may use one or more collection instruments to receive the data (e.g. personal or telephone interviews; paper, electronic or web questionnaires; SDMX web services). Collection instruments may also be data extraction routines used to gather data from existing statistical or administrative registers (e.g. by using existing service interfaces). This sub-process also includes preparing and testing the contents and functioning of that collection instrument (e.g. cognitive testing of the questions in a questionnaire). It is recommended to consider the direct connection of collection instruments to a metadata system, so that metadata can be more easily captured in the collection phase. Connecting metadata and data at the point of capture can save work in later phases. Capturing the metrics of data collection (paradata) is also an important consideration in this sub-process for calculating and analysing process quality indicators.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process describes the activities to build and reuse the collection instruments needed during the Collect phase. Subject matter sponsors are solely responsible for specifying and certifying collection instrument requirements. The actual rendering or building of the instrument is performed by a single accountable centre, which leverages AI and automation to produce survey instruments or extraction routines rapidly and at scale. Automated instrument building enables the strict enforcement of timeliness standards (such as a maximum allowed period between specification and instrument launch), with policies and procedures reformed to reflect these new practices. Direct connection of collection instruments to metadata systems is required to ensure seamless data and metadata capture at source. Staff roles and responsibilities are clearly delineated, removing ambiguity and supporting the rapid, standardized, and high-quality development of instruments for all relevant data acquisition needs.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: Updates require the 'subject matter sponsor' to be solely responsible for specification and certification of collection instruments, and a 'single designated centre' to handle their rendering using AI/automation. The 'Operations Officer', whose key activities include 'participates in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of manual and automated operations for the collection, coding and processing of data,' and providing 'assistance and advice to users on methods and practices of collection and coding', will be primarily focused on the operational aspect—implementing, adapting, and supporting the transition to single-centre, AI-driven rapid instrument creation and enforcing timeline and automation policies. Their knowledge of both manual and digital collection processes will be crucial for ensuring compliance, quality, and timely instrument delivery.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Configure workflows
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process configures the workflows, systems and transformations used within the business processes, from data collection through to dissemination. In this sub-process, the workflows are configured based on the design created in sub-process 2.6 (Design production systems and workflows). This could include modifying a standardised workflow for a specific purpose, assembling the workflows for the different phases together (possibly with a workflow/business process management system) and configuring systems accordingly.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process configures the workflows, systems, and transformations used within all business processes—from data collection through to dissemination—to form modular, automation-ready data pipelines. Workflows are assembled, customized, and deployed using digital workflow or business process management platforms, with extensive AI/automation support for orchestration, process monitoring, and autonomous task triggering. These workflows enable seamless, hands-free movement of data and outputs between business process stages, allowing real-time responsiveness and minimizing the need for manual intervention. Human involvement is limited to oversight, rapid workflow adaptation where unique business needs arise, and exception escalation that cannot be managed automatically.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: Configuration must now focus on 'full automation, AI-powered orchestration and monitoring, seamless modular integration,' and 'real-time responsive data movement.' The 'Operations Officer' is implicated, as their traditional involvement in 'designing the specifications for testing of applications, the application and conversion of databases, and the maintenance and use of databases' is now shaped by digital configuration and orchestration tools. They ensure that workflow configuration achieves compatibility with modern automation standards, supports effective exception management, and enables real-time responsiveness.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Test production systems
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process is concerned with the testing of assembled and configured services and related workflows. It includes technical testing and sign-off of new programmes and routines, as well as confirmation that existing routines from other statistical business processes are suitable for use in this case. Whilst part of this activity concerning the testing of individual components and services could logically be linked with sub-processes 3.1 (Reuse or build collection instruments), 3.2 (Reuse or build processing and analysis components) and 3.3 (Reuse or build dissemination components), this sub-process also includes testing of interactions between assembled and configured services and ensuring that the whole production solution works in a coherent way. It can also include arranging secure channels for the transmission of the data, checking detailed information about files and metadata with a data supplier and receiving test files to assess if data are fit for use.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process is focused on testing the assembled and configured services and workflows by employing automated, AI-powered continuous testing practices. All new programs, routines, and workflow interactions are subject to automated regression and functional tests, with self-testing and monitoring embedded in all integrated components. Testing of data flows, file structure, metadata, and secure transmission is handled primarily by automated pipelines, with full audit trails and auto-generated reports to support later analysis or compliance. Human involvement is reserved for critical sign-off, investigating failed or ambiguous automated tests, managing complex escalations, and verifying regulatory or policy compliance. This approach enables faster, more reliable go-live decisions, reduces operational risk, and assures resilient deployment of production solutions.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: With 'AI-powered self-testing, regression suites, and system audits' being standard, the 'Operations Officer' who 'analyses and prepares reports... on how the survey was conducted, problems encountered in implementing concepts, definitions, classifications and other instructions, and recommending alternatives,' will now focus on analysis of automated test results, escalation of issues, and high-level oversight of automated go-live decisions—moving away from manual testing toward process supervision.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Test statistical business process
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process describes the activities to manage a field test or pilot of the statistical business process. Typically, it includes a small-scale data collection, to test the collection instruments, followed by processing and analysis of the collected data, to ensure the statistical business process performs as expected. Following the pilot, it may be necessary to go back to a previous step and make adjustments to collection instruments, systems or components. For a major statistical business process, e.g. a population census, there may be several iterations until the process is working satisfactorily.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process manages a field test or pilot of the statistical business process using automated orchestration and AI-driven monitoring to execute, track, and analyze pilot runs. All pilot phases—from collection instrument validation through end-to-end process testing—are tracked through digital platforms that automate data collection, process monitoring, and initial results analysis. Iterative feedback, result synthesis, and suggested improvements are generated by automated and AI-supported systems, enabling automatic identification of issues, process optimization, and faster cycling between iterations. Human experts supervise the piloting phase, make decisions regarding significant process re-designs, and provide final sign-off for transition to live operational status.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: AI-driven orchestration, monitoring, and iterative analysis of pilot runs are now emphasized. The 'Operations Officer' ('analyzes reported data and work results and prepares reports... on how the survey was conducted, problems encountered, recommending alternatives') will supervise digital pilot execution, review AI-generated monitoring reports, escalate significant process failures, and support design iteration based on pilot results.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Finalise production systems
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process includes the activities to put the assembled and configured processes and services, including modified and newly-created services, into production ready for use. The activities include: Producing documentation about the process components, including technical documentation and user manuals; Training the users of the system on how to operate the process; Moving the process components into the production environment and ensuring they work as expected in that environment (this activity may also be part of sub-process 3.5 (Test production systems).
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process finalises and deploys the assembled and configured processes and services—including all modified and newly-created systems—into production, utilizing automated deployment and orchestration tools to ensure readiness. Digital and AI-powered solutions generate all required documentation (technical manuals, user guides, change logs) automatically, and facilitate user onboarding and training via interactive platforms and digital learning modules. Live deployment is monitored and verified through automated tests and real-time telemetry, with issues escalated for human review only in exception cases. Manual staff activities focus on oversight, compliance validation, and approval of production readiness, ensuring the highest standards of operational efficiency and reliability.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: GSBPM updates require 'automated deployment, digital documentation, and AI-assisted user onboarding/training.' The 'Operations Officer', whose tasks include 'writes survey information manuals, training packages, monitoring procedures and management reports' and 'provides input to training materials concerning data collection operations and assists in training delivery,' will now be responsible for reviewing and supplementing automated system documentation, facilitating digital onboarding, and overseeing the automated move to production. Their expertise is essential for validation and compliance review.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Collect
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This phase collects or gathers all necessary information (e.g. data, metadata and paradata), using different collection approaches (e.g. acquisition, collection, extraction, transfer), and loads them into the appropriate environment for further processing. Whilst it can include validation of data set formats, it does not include any transformations of the data themselves, as these are all done in the Process phase. For statistical outputs produced regularly, this phase occurs in each iteration. The Collect phase is broken down into four sub-processes (Figure 10), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This phase collects or gathers all necessary information (data, metadata, paradata) using digitally orchestrated, automation-enabled, and AI-supported systems. Passive data acquisition—from administrative, digital, and system-byproduct sources—is the default and preferred mode, utilizing APIs, automated feeds, and seamless system integrations wherever possible. Active, respondent-driven collection (e.g., surveys) is only used when passive sources are insufficient and must be minimized and justified. All collection methods are subject to real-time intake, validation, and traceability, with human involvement focused on exception handling, compliance oversight, and critical data quality control. The Collect phase is broken into four sub-processes (Figure 10), which can occur sequentially, in parallel, and iteratively, with automation maximizing efficiency and speed in each iteration.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The updated GSBPM stresses digital orchestration, automation, and AI support for data intake, making passive data acquisition (administrative, digital, automated feeds) the default. The 'Operations Officer'—who 'participates in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of manual and automated operations for the collection, coding and processing of data' and 'provides assistance and advice to users on methods and practices of collection and coding'—will shift from hands-on manual or operational collection to oversight, troubleshooting, exception handling, and continuous improvement of digitalized and automated collection systems. They will need to validate that automation is functioning correctly, investigate exceptions, and ensure compliance with new passive-oriented approaches.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Set up collection
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process ensures that the people, processes and technology (e.g. web-based applications, devices to be used in collection, communication channels) are ready to collect data and metadata, as designed. It takes place over a period of time, as it includes the strategy, planning and training activities in preparation for the specific instance of the statistical business process. Where the process is repeated regularly, some (or all) of these activities may not be explicitly required for each iteration. For one-off and new processes, these activities can be lengthy. For survey data, this sub-process includes: Training collection staff; Training system using supervised machine learning techniques; Ensuring collection resources are available (e.g. collection devices, apps, APIs); Agreeing on terms with any intermediate collection bodies, (e.g. sub-contractors for computer assisted telephone interviewing, web service providers); Configuring collection systems to request and receive the data, including location data; Ensuring the security of data to be collected; Preparing collection instruments (e.g. printing questionnaires, pre-filling them with existing data, loading questionnaires and data onto interviewers' devices/computers, APIs, web scraping tools); Providing information for respondents (e.g. drafting letters/emails to respondents, credentials, guidance or tailored information to address questions they may have, or notifying respondents when online reporting instruments will be made available); Translation of materials (e.g. into the different languages spoken or used in the country). For non-survey sources, this sub-process ensures that the necessary processes, systems and confidentiality procedures are in place, to receive or extract the necessary information from the source. This includes: Evaluating requests to obtain the data and logging the request in a centralised inventory; Initiating contacts with organisations providing the data, and sending an introductory package with details on the process of obtaining the data; Routine checks that the system is working as expected.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process ensures that all people, processes, and technologies (e.g., apps, APIs, devices) are optimally configured to collect data and metadata, as designed, with a strong focus on automation, metadata compliance, and resource flexibility. Routine use of automation is required for recurring data acquisitions and ingestion partnerships. Minimum metadata standards must be checked and validated for every collection or acquisition, with AI-enabled tools applied to extract structured data from unstructured sources and to verify data source credibility—reducing misinformation and ensuring fitness for application. All setup activities also support a 'one workforce' model: staff are cross-trained for multiple roles and resource pools are dynamically allocated or reallocated in real time, based on AI-driven or demand-responsive input, providing greater efficiency and adaptability. For non-survey as well as survey sources, these principles support readiness, quality, and scalability by default.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The sub-process now requires 'routine use of automation for recurring data acquisitions and ingestion partnerships,' 'minimum metadata standards,' and support for a 'one workforce' model. The 'Operations Officer' role is emphasized because it includes 'participates in the implementation, conduct and maintenance of... automated operations,' 'prepares reports and recommendations outlining options and requirements for the operation of statistical collection and processing systems,' and 'provides input to training materials concerning data collection operations and assists in training delivery.' Now, their tasks will focus on: ensuring automated and AI-enabled systems are properly set up, verifying compliance with metadata standards, participating in flexible workforce allocation, and supporting training/resource adaptation for dynamic, digital-first environments.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Run collection
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process is where the collection is implemented. The different collection instruments are used to collect or gather the information, which may include raw microdata or aggregates produced at the source, as well as any associated metadata. For survey or census data, it can include: Initial contact with respondents to request data and any subsequent follow-up or reminder actions, recording when and how they were contacted, and whether they have reacted; Management of the relationship between the statistical organisation and respondents, so that it remains positive, and recording and responding to comments, queries and complaints. (Minimisation of the number of non-respondents contributes significantly to higher quality of the collected data.); Manual data entry at the point of contact, or fieldwork management, depending on the source and collection approach; Georeferencing at the same time as collection of the data (using inputs from location-enabled systems such as GPS), or recording location by putting a mark on a map, etc., depending on the geographical frame and the technology used. Automated logical checks on data at the point of collection (i.e. validation-on-entry for survey response data) are considered to take place in 5.3 (Review and validate). For administrative, geospatial, or other non-statistical data, the data supplier either sends it as scheduled or is contacted to send the information, which might require follow-ups. Broader technical-level engagement with data suppliers falls under the Data Supplier Management overarching activity. In the case where the data are published under an Open Data license and exist in machine-readable form, they may be freely accessed and used. This sub-process may also include the monitoring of data collection and making any necessary changes to improve data quality. This includes generating reports, visualising and adjusting the process for obtaining data to ensure the data are fit for use. When the collection meets its targets, it is closed and a report on the collection is produced. Some basic checks of the structure and integrity of the information received may take place within this sub-process, (e.g. checking that files are in the right format and contain the expected fields).
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process implements data collection via a digital-first, automation-driven model, prioritizing passive, system-based, and administrative data pipelines wherever possible. Recurring external data acquisitions are orchestrated through automated scheduling and digital APIs; AI/ML tools auto-populate and validate metadata repositories and perform information management tagging as soon as data is ingested. For survey or respondent-dependent cases, AI/ML-enabled platforms optimize assignment of contacts and resources in real time—dynamically prioritizing, balancing workloads, and reallocating a single, cross-trained resource pool to improve efficiency and data quality. Manual or active contact methods are only pursued when passive collection is not feasible or complete. Continuous digital monitoring, exception reporting, and process-adjustment mechanisms further support collection quality. Human staff are primarily tasked with exception resolution, oversight, and process improvement based on analytics and feedback.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: This sub-process must now provide 'AI-driven, real-time case management, workload balancing, and dynamic reallocation of resources,' prioritizing passive, automated data acquisition. The 'Operations Officer'—trained in both manual and automated system operation—will oversee deployment, monitor performance, support collection optimization through AI/automation dashboards, and engage in exception resolution and efficiency review. Their role is more supervisory, adaptive, and quality-focused, minimizing hands-on manual work in favor of digital oversight.
